item.title: Tech Companies Promote AI in Schools Amid Growing Educational Scrutiny
item.description:
Tech Companies Promote AI in Schools Amid Growing Educational Scrutiny

AI companies are currently pitching schools on the necessity of generative AI, providing resources and curricula—often pro bono—to ensure students do not fall behind in a competitive job market.

💡 Why it matters

According to New York Times education technology reporter Natasha Singer, this approach mirrors how the tech industry has built influence in classrooms for 15 years. In her book Coding Kids, Singer details how companies promoted computer science as a ticket to high-paying jobs while training students on their specific software to create future customers.

⚙️ Key details

Historically, major tech companies have integrated their tools directly into educational systems:

Company Educational Tool/Method
Apple Swift curricula for AP Computer Science Principles
Microsoft Minecraft curricula for AP Computer Science Principles
Google Chromebooks and the Classroom app
Code.org “Hour of Code” campaign and celebrity-led videos

🔍 Current Status

While AI companies continue their push, several developments indicate increasing pushback:

  • School Bans: New York City has banned AI use in elementary and middle schools for the coming year, and Los Angeles has implemented broader restrictions including high schoolers.
  • Hardware Shifts: Some schools are removing Google Chromebooks.
  • Academic Findings: Global research indicates that adding technology to the classroom often does not have a significant impact on actual learning.
  • Graduate Feedback: Some recent graduates report feeling let down after being told to code their whole lives, only to find diminishing entry-level jobs.

#AI #Education #EdTech #ComputerScience

Source: Schools are catching on to Big Tech’s playbook

item.title: Microsoft agrees to enforceable AI privacy and safety principles for school districts
item.description:
Microsoft agrees to enforceable AI privacy and safety principles for school districts

Microsoft has reached a new agreement regarding AI privacy and safety rules for schools, establishing legally enforceable principles for districts that adopt them. The commitment follows a week after major school systems in New York City and Los Angeles implemented one-year bans on student-facing AI tools to allow time to establish proper guardrails.

🔍 Overview

Microsoft entered into this agreement with the American Federation of Teachers (AFT) and its New York City affiliate, the United Federation of Teachers (UFT). The terms include ten principles that school districts can choose to add to their contracts. AFT President Randi Weingarten described the terms as “iron-clad” and necessary because “no one else, including the federal government, has stepped up to do the real work.”

⚙️ Key details

The agreement establishes specific data protections and operational requirements for Microsoft’s AI tools in educational settings:

Principle Requirement
Model Training No training of AI models on student or educator data
Data Collection Limits the initial amount of data Microsoft collects
Transparency Disclosing how tools work to families in plain language
AI Companions Prohibits the use of AI companions
Risk Management Requires human review for “high-risk” decisions

💡 Why it matters

As some parents and educators resist the use of screens and AI in schools, Microsoft is responding to a policy crackdown. The AFT has been critical of tech in schools, with President Weingarten previously calling for a ban on screens before third grade and student-facing AI before middle school. However, the organization is also working with tech companies, including a $23 million AI training hub for educators funded by Anthropic, Microsoft, and OpenAI.

🚀 Availability

Starting in November, school districts can opt to add these new terms to existing or new agreements. The process is designed so districts do not have to renegotiate their entire contracts to include these protections.

#Microsoft #EdTech #AFT #AIPrivacy #Education

Source: Microsoft has new AI privacy rules for schools

item.title: OECD Study Finds Students Using AI Perform Worse Without Critical Assessment Training
item.description:
OECD Study Finds Students Using AI Perform Worse Without Critical Assessment Training

According to newly released data from the OECD’s Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), students who use artificial intelligence to help them study tend to perform worse at school than those who do not. The study, which collected data in 2025, represents the first time PISA has evaluated student performance since AI tools went truly mainstream.

📊 Scope of the study

The PISA study evaluated 15-year-old students across science, math, and reading. Key findings regarding student demographics and global trends include:

  • Global scale: The data draws from over 760,000 students across 91 countries.
  • Socioeconomic factors: After adjusting for socioeconomic status, students who never use AI generally outperformed those who do in science. AI use was found to be more common among students from relatively advantaged backgrounds, which likely reflects better access to hardware, stable internet access, and paid AI tools.
  • Geographic variation: AI utilization varies widely by country. For example, over 95 percent of Vietnamese students reported using AI tools, compared to just 60 percent in Japan.
  • Curiosity connection: The study noted that student curiosity levels correlate with AI use, peaking among daily users.

⚙️ Performance by AI task and frequency

The relationship between AI use and academic performance is complex, with results heavily dependent on how and how often the tools are used.

Method of AI Use Performance Impact
Summarizing texts or drafting writing assignments Relatively worse performance
Preliminary research or broad “help me learn” use Less of a performance drop
Weekly use to generally help learn Outperformed non-users (though not by much)
Weekly general help + critical assessment training All regular users outperformed non-users

Frequency of use also plays a significant role in student outcomes:

  • Daily or yearly use: Students who used AI daily, as well as those who only used it once or twice a year, tended to perform the worst.
  • Weekly or monthly use: Better academic results were seen among monthly or weekly AI users.

💡 Intentional learning vs. shortcutting

The study’s authors suggest that “moderate and intentional use of AI for schoolwork and learning” could have positive effects, especially when students are trained to critically assess the information they receive.

OECD director of learning and skills Andreas Schleicher explained the cognitive dynamics of using technology in education:

“In the same way that we do not become fit by watching sports but by doing sports, learning does not occur through the consumption of content, but as a productive cognitive struggle of the mind with new material,” Schleicher wrote. “Where technology enables or enhances that cognitive struggle, students will advance.”

Conversely, Schleicher added: “Where technology short-circuits the productive struggle of learning, it will undercut students’ development.”

#PISA #OECD #EdTech #AIinEducation

Source: Students who use AI generally score worse at school

item.title: Prompt-engineering framework enables personalized responses for AI teaching assistants
item.description:
Prompt-engineering framework enables personalized responses for AI teaching assistants

A new study presents a prompt-engineering-based framework designed to personalize general-purpose LLM/RAG-based AI teaching assistants, such as Jill Watson, across various academic courses and disciplines.

🧩 How it works

The framework adapts AI responses by utilizing six specific dimensions related to the learner:

  • Self-assessment
  • Abstraction preference
  • Verbosity preference
  • Perceptual orientation
  • Information processing style
  • Level of understanding

These dimensions allow for the creation of 96 distinct learner profiles. Additionally, student queries are analyzed using Bloom’s Taxonomy to estimate the cognitive complexity of each interaction. This data is encoded into structured prompts that condition the LLM, enabling adaptive behavior without the need for model retraining.

⚙️ Key details

The framework was evaluated through both NLP metrics and a human study involving five participants. Results indicate:

  • Perceived differences in the structure and style of responses across personalization conditions.
  • Statistical evidence identifying specific learner attributes that correlate with measurable changes in AI output.

💡 Why it matters

These findings provide preliminary evidence that prompt-based personalization can effectively support adaptive behavior in LLM-powered educational agents, allowing for tailored interactions within an academic context.

#AI #LLM #EdTech #PromptEngineering #RAG

Source: A Prompt-Engineering Approach to Develop Scalable, Flexible, and Real-Time Hybrid Micro-Level Personalization in a General Purpose AI Teaching Assistant

item.title: University Startups Launches Trinity AI to Assist Students with Disability Transition Planning
item.description:
University Startups Launches Trinity AI to Assist Students with Disability Transition Planning

Trinity is a conversational AI solution developed by University Startups to assist students with disabilities in taking ownership of their postsecondary and Individualized Education Program (IEP) planning.

🧩 How it works

University Startups utilized g/d/n/a to build a fully serverless architecture on AWS. The system utilizes a multi-agent solution powered by Amazon Bedrock and Claude 3.5 Sonnet to provide targeted guidance.

The architecture employs a hierarchical six-agent system:

Agent Function
Orchestrator Agent Reads student conversation, selects the right path, sequences agents, and consolidates final output
College Agent Recommends 4-year universities and community colleges from an over 30,000 record Knowledge Base
Employment Agent Matches jobs and career pathways from an over 1,000 occupation Knowledge Base
Training Agent Recommends vocational programs and certifications

⚙️ Key details

The platform includes accessibility features such as Amazon Polly for text-to-speech and Amazon Transcribe for speech-to-text. Data security is maintained through compliance with HIPAA and FERPA standards, while Amazon Bedrock Guardrails are used for content filtering and hallucination reduction.

🚀 Availability

Trinity reached educators and students across more than a dozen U.S. states within its first year. International expansion into Saudi Arabia and Kuwait is now underway.

#ArtificialIntelligence #EdTech #AWS #Accessibility #SpecialEducation

Source: Trinity: Agentic AI-powered transition planning for students with disabilities | Amazon Web Services

item.title: New York City Bans Classroom AI Use for Students Until High School
item.description:
New York City Bans Classroom AI Use for Students Until High School

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has announced a new policy that will ban younger schoolchildren from using AI in classrooms. The one-year moratorium, effective in the 2026-2027 school year, will impact about 600,000 public school students in 2-K through eighth grade.

⚙️ Key Details

The new rules introduced by NYC’s Department of Education establish strict boundaries on technology inside classrooms:

  • AI Classroom Ban: Students are kept from using AI in classrooms until they enter high school.
  • Companion Chatbots: Chatbots designed specifically for companionship and mental support are banned across all grades.
  • Grading Restrictions: Teachers are barred from using AI tools to grade assignments.
  • Device and Screen Limits: Individual screen use is banned until third grade. The department is also issuing recommended screen time limits, including a maximum of 45 minutes per day for middle schoolers.
  • Device Ban Context: These changes follow NYC’s public school system introducing a bell-to-bell ban on personal internet-enabled electronic devices, including smartphones, for the 2025-2026 school year.

🧩 Exceptions and High School Rules

High school students will only be permitted to use AI in specific instances. To support this transition, they will be offered AI literacy classes twice a year to help them “think critically” before they come to “rely on it.”

Exceptions to the ban may be granted for:

  • AI tools that help students with disabilities or multilingual students.
  • Particular purposes like computer science programs.
  • Teachers using AI for lesson planning.

🧪 Limited AI Pilot Program

A “limited AI pilot” program will also be offered at up to five classes in a “small number” of high school classrooms. This program will feature tools vetted to meet safety and data privacy standards while “keeping students as the primary thinker.” These tools feature set time limits for usage and include:

Tool Purpose
Quill English language support
Edia Math
Brisk Teaching Guiding study practice
Playlab Multi-subject support
Intel AI-Ready Schools Multi-subject support

💡 Why It Matters

NYC district leaders state that the new classroom AI moratorium is one of the most restrictive policies in the US. However, countries such as Norway, Sweden, and the Netherlands have implemented nationwide changes to address similar concerns about how technology impacts developing minds.

“Children need teachers and human connection in order to learn and grow. They need to develop skills alongside their peers, build relationships with educators, and wrestle with tough problems on their own,” Mamdani said in a statement. “The tech industry wants us to believe that AI-powered early education is not only inevitable, but necessary. We do not see it that way.”

#NYCPublicSchools #AIEducation #EdTech

Source: NYC bans AI use for students until they reach high school
